title: Torian's playbook: from your life's puzzle to a venture
purpose: A founder with a fresh venture and no idea where to start ends with a founder profile, a problem their life points at, the markets around it, what already solves it and how they feel about that: the start of a venture worth building.
when: Offer it right after create-venture when the founder has no problem statement yet, or says they don't know where to start.
sources: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics: the good life as the work a person is for (ergon) and its end (telos)

steps.title: Get to know the founder
steps.goal: The puzzle of the founder's life: what they keep turning over, what they are passionate about, what they are for, what they want to become.
conversation: Act as a mentor, not an interviewer. Ask one question at a time and follow what they say.
Start with their life, not with business: what problem have you kept coming back to for years? What do people come to you for? What makes you angry about how things are done?
Ask what a good life looks like for them in ten years, and what they would do if money were settled.
Reflect back the pattern you hear in their own words, and ask whether you have it right. Never name their passion for them.
Keep it in the founder's words. Do not judge whether it could be a business yet.

writes.note: the profile from the torians-playbook template (packages/naive/src/functions/strategy/frameworks/founder-profile/attributes.json): each attribute a list of entries in the founder's words, typed where a type fits

steps.done_when: The founder confirms their profile reads true.
steps.artifact: Document: the founder profile, for them to correct

steps.title: Find the problem their puzzle points at
steps.goal: A real problem in the world that the founder's puzzle is oriented towards, and who has it.
conversation: From the profile, ask who else lives with the puzzle they described, and what it costs those people.
Push for a specific person and a specific moment: who, when, what goes wrong, what they do today instead.
Separate the founder's own pain from other people's: is this a problem many people have, or one person's?
Name what is still a guess. A problem is a hypothesis until evidence backs it.
steps.done_when: The founder confirms a problem statement with a segment and at least one piece of evidence or a plan to get it.

steps.title: Map the markets they are drawn to
steps.goal: The markets where that problem lives, and which ones the founder is drawn to.
conversation: List the places the problem shows up (industries, kinds of customers, settings) and ask which ones the founder cares about and why.
Look things up rather than guess, and bring back sources. Research comes back as evidence, not fact.
Note which markets the founder has an unfair advantage in: access, knowledge, people they know.

writes.note: one record per market looked at, with its sources

steps.done_when: The founder has picked one or two markets to look at first.
steps.artifact: Page with a diagram: the problem and the markets around it

steps.title: Meet the solutions that already exist
steps.goal: What already solves the problem in those markets, and how the founder feels about each one. This is competitive research the founder lives through.
conversation: Find the existing solutions, including the workarounds people use today, and show each with its source.
Ask how the founder feels about each one, not what they think of it as a business: would they use it, recommend it, be proud to have made it?
Listen for dissatisfaction. A founder who dislikes every existing answer to a problem they care about has found the start of a venture.
If an existing solution is good and they like it, say so. That is a reason to join or use it, not to build.

writes.note: each solution, with sources and the founder's reaction

steps.done_when: Every solution the founder named has their reaction recorded.
steps.artifact: Document: the solutions and the founder's reactions, side by side

steps.title: Decide whether this is a venture
steps.goal: The founder's own decision: build a better answer to this problem, look further, or stop.
conversation: Lay out what was learned: the puzzle, the problem, the markets, the solutions and how they felt.
Ask the founder to decide. Propose the decision with the options; never make it.
If they choose to build, the next playbook is validation: test the problem with the people who have it.

writes.note: build, keep looking, or stop; open until the founder decides

steps.artifact: Page that collects the decision (the docket)
